title: A biodiversity hotspot is defined by what it has lost
sources: Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF), 'Biodiversity hotspots' (criteria; 36 hotspots)
India's four hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats, Sundaland (Nicobar Islands) (Padhai; Maps for UPSC)
Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972: protected-area categories (WII ENVIS page); national park and sanctuary rules (GKToday; WildTrails)

quiz.q: Which hotspot covers the Nicobar Islands?
quiz.why: Right. India's part of the Sundaland hotspot is the Nicobar Islands; the Andamans fall in Indo-Burma.

script: A biodiversity hotspot isn't just rich in species.
It's defined by what it has lost.
To qualify, a region needs at least 1,500 plant species found nowhere else,
To qualify, a region needs at least fifteen hundred plant species found nowhere else,
and must have lost at least 70 percent of its original vegetation.
and must have lost at least seventy percent of its original vegetation.
There are 36 worldwide.
There are thirty-six worldwide.
Four reach into India:
the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, the Western Ghats,
and Sundaland, through the Nicobar Islands.
But a hotspot is a conservation label, not a law.
Legal protection comes from the Wild Life Protection Act:
national parks, sanctuaries, conservation reserves and community reserves.
In a national park, grazing is not allowed.
In a sanctuary, the Chief Wildlife Warden can permit some rights.
Rich, and threatened,
by definition.
Your turn.
Which hotspot covers the Nicobar Islands?

right.label: Sanctuary
right.text: Some rights, if the Warden permits

claims.claim: A hotspot must contain at least 1,500 (1500) species of vascular plants found nowhere else and have lost at least 70 percent of its primary native vegetation; there are 36 hotspots
Four hotspots include parts of India: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats (and Sri Lanka), and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands)
Hotspot criteria were formalised by Conservation International (a conservation framework, not a legal designation in India)
Protected areas under the Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972 include national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, conservation reserves and community reserves (1972)
No grazing is allowed in national parks; in sanctuaries, certain rights may be allowed at the discretion of the Chief Wildlife Warden

review_note: Hotspot criteria from CEPF (the hotspot programme's funder) plus an explainer; the 1,500 figure refers to endemic vascular plants. India's four hotspots from two explainers. The sanctuary-rights point (Chief Wildlife Warden's discretion) is in one source only (GKToday); check against WLPA sections 33 and 35. Protected-area counts are deliberately left out: the WII page is dated 2021 and its totals don't add up. Andamans are in Indo-Burma per Maps for UPSC; that supports the quiz explanation.
